summary.text: A mangrove is a shrub or tree that grows mainly in salty or brackish coastal water, mostly on tropical and subtropical coasts.
Special adaptations let mangroves take in extra oxygen and remove salt, so they tolerate conditions that kill most plants.
Mangrove forests protect nearby areas from tsunamis and extreme weather, and they are effective at storing carbon.

items.prompt: Black mangroves send up straw-like roots that poke out of the mud. Why?

options.label: To catch falling leaves as food
To get air the soggy mud lacks
To soak up rainwater to drink
To spread their seeds further

items.explain: Waterlogged mangrove soil holds little free oxygen, so these pneumatophores stick up like straws to take gases straight from the air.

items.prompt: A storm surge is heading for two stretches of coast. Which one is likely better protected?

options.label: The one cleared for an open sandy beach
The one with a row of beach houses
The one with a wide mangrove forest
The one dug out for fish ponds

items.explain: Mangroves protect nearby areas from tsunamis and extreme weather events.

items.prompt: Mangrove species come from several unrelated plant families, yet they share similar features. Why?

options.label: They all descend from one recent ancestor
Farmers crossbred them over the centuries
They swap genes by sharing pollen
Each evolved similar fixes for the same conditions

items.explain: This is convergent evolution: unrelated species found similar solutions to variable salinity, flooding, airless soils and intense sun.

items.prompt: Which continent reported no mangrove area at all in 2025?

options.label: Europe
Africa
South America
Asia

items.explain: Europe reported no mangrove area, while Asia had the largest area at 6.10 million hectares.

items.prompt: The red mangrove lives where seawater covers it most often. How does it get air?

options.label: Its leaves pull oxygen out of seawater
Stilt roots lift it up and its bark takes in air
It stores air inside a hollow trunk
It floats its leaves flat on the water

items.explain: The red mangrove props itself above the water on stilt or prop roots and absorbs air through pores called lenticels in its bark.

items.prompt: In some places evaporation makes the water saltier than the open ocean. How salty can the water get where mangroves still grow?

options.label: About as salty as seawater
About half as salty as seawater
Over twice as salty as seawater
About ten times as salty as seawater

items.explain: Various mangrove species tolerate water concentrated by evaporation to over twice the salinity of ocean seawater, up to 9%.

paragraphs.heading: What a mangrove is
paragraphs.text: A mangrove is a shrub or tree that lives mainly in salty or brackish water along the coast. The same word is used for the tropical coastal vegetation made up of such plants. Mangroves line coastlines and tidal rivers in tropical and subtropical regions around the world. Most grow between 30° N and 30° S, and the largest areas lie within 5° of the equator. They are halophytic, which means salt-tolerant.

paragraphs.heading: Living in salt and mud
paragraphs.text: Mangrove shores are hard places for plants. The mud is always waterlogged, so it holds little free oxygen, and bacteria in it give off nitrogen gas, sulfides and methane that leave the soil much less nourishing. The water can range from brackish, through ordinary seawater at 3 to 4% salt, to pools so concentrated by evaporation that they reach 9%. Mangroves cope with an elaborate system for filtering out salt and an elaborate set of roots that handles both saltwater and waves. These adaptations let them take in extra oxygen and shed salt where most plants would die.

paragraphs.heading: Roots that breathe
paragraphs.text: Different mangroves solve the oxygen problem in different ways. The red mangrove grows in the most flooded spots, lifts itself above the water on stilt or prop roots, and takes in air through lenticels in its bark. The black mangrove lives on higher ground and sends up pneumatophores, root-like structures that poke out of the mud like straws for breathing. These tubes usually reach up to 30 cm, and in some species more than 3 m. Through them mangroves absorb gases straight from the air, and nutrients such as iron from the poor soil.

paragraphs.heading: Many families, one way of life
paragraphs.text: Mangroves do not form a single plant family. Plants from several families arrived at the same way of life through convergent evolution, finding similar answers to shifting salt levels, tidal flooding, oxygen-poor soils and strong sun. About 70 species in 20 genera from 16 families count as true mangroves, plants found almost only in mangrove habitats. Any one mangrove stand usually has few plant species, but the greatest variety is in Southeast Asia, above all the Indonesian islands. Mangrove plant families first appeared between the Late Cretaceous and the Paleocene, and the oldest known mangrove palm fossils are 75 million years old.

paragraphs.heading: Why they matter
paragraphs.text: Mangroves help keep coastal and marine ecosystems going. They shield nearby land from tsunamis and extreme weather, and they are good at capturing and storing carbon. In 2025 the world's mangroves covered an estimated 15.9 million hectares. Asia holds the most, at 6.10 million hectares, while Europe reported none. Indonesia alone has 3.40 million hectares, and together with Brazil, Australia, Nigeria and Mexico it holds almost half of all mangroves.

paragraphs.heading: Loss and restoration
paragraphs.text: Since 2010, remote sensing and global data have been used to track how much mangrove exists and how fast it is being cleared. A 2022 study estimated a net loss of 3,700 km² of mangroves worldwide between 1999 and 2019. Human activity keeps removing them, at about 0.16% a year globally and up to 0.70% a year in some countries, and the forests that remain are also losing quality. Restoration draws interest, but its success may depend on working closely with local people and on checking that the chosen species will suit the site.
